newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, dollar jump, but bonds fall.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, dollar jump, but bonds fall.

text.p: Stocks rose for a second day Wednesday as investors snapped up technology shares again, but bonds fell for the third straight session after a disappointing two-year Treasury note auction.
The dollar rose against the Swiss franc, which slumped to its lowest level in nearly two years as Switzerland's economy showed more signs of distress.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 38.44 points at 6,346.77, adding to Tuesday's rally of nearly 40 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,572 to 927 on active volume of 500 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
International Business Machines Corp. led the blue chips, surging $6.875 to $158.75, contributing more than half the Dow index's advance.
"Stocks are in a year-end window-dressing rally and IBM is the one all the money managers want in their portfolios," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
The technology-laced Nasdaq Composite index jumped 19.06 points to 1,285.38.
Analysts said the market was showing some early signs of the so-called Santa Claus rally, the late December advance that stocks enjoy nearly every year.
"My suspicion is that we're looking at the early part of it," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "This is a classic time of year when the market has an upside bias."

The rally broadened considerably over Tuesday, but analysts reckoned that a sustained rise was unlikely until the market steers clear of the late-year portfolio shifting by money managers and the specter of Friday's triple-witching expiration of futures, index options and stock options.
"Is this the start of a new breakout? Probably not," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co.

"I wouldn't read too much into it because it's hard to distinguish what's going on in the last days of a year and it's an options expirations week," he said. "Plus, interest rates are still high and that's a challenge for stocks."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond lost half a point, raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, to 6.70 percent from 6.66 percent at Tuesday's close.
"This can't go on forever," said Barthel. "There's a very good correlation that says when interest rates go up, the market pays the penalty."
The dollar climbed to 1.3340 Swiss francs, its highest since early January 1995, before settling late Wednesday at 1.3295 Swiss, up from 1.3260 late Tuesday.
The dollar also rose to a high of 1.5552 German marks, closing at 1.5517, up from 1.5500 late Tuesday. It fell to 113.69 Japanese yen from 113.87 yen.
Crude oil prices hit a new post-Gulf War high as worries about low heating oil stocks outweighed weather forecasts that said a cold front headed for New England would be milder than expected.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange crude for January delivery settled up 45 cents at $26.16 a barrel and rose as high $26.20 in late trading, eclipsing the old post-Gulf War high of $26.10 made on Oct. 22.
January heating oil finished up 0.64 cent a gallon at 74.18 cents while January gasoline settled up 1.40 cents at 71.17 cents a gallon.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index finished 38.6 points higher at 4,018.2, regaining the 4,000 level for the first time in five days. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average ended down 320.43 points at 20,093.03, the day's low.
